claim: Sixteen human participants performed a predictive-inference task while fMRI was used to measure their blood-oxygenation-level-dependent (BOLD) brain activity.
source: Sixteen human participants performed a predictive-inference task (Figure 1A) while fMRI was used to measure their blood-oxygenation-level-dependent (BOLD) brain activity.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of participants and the experimental procedure.

claim: The task required participants to predict the location of a single rewarded target from a circular array of ten targets.
source: The task required them to predict the location of a single rewarded target from a circular array of ten targets.
evidence: The manuscript describes the task structure.

claim: In the noisy condition, the rewarded target would appear in one of the five locations relative to the location of the current best target, and the hazard rate was low (H = 0.02).
source: In the noisy condition (Figure 1B–C), the rewarded target would appear in one of the five locations relative to the location of the current best target, and the hazard rate was low (H = 0.02).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the parameters of the noisy condition and references Figure 1B-C.

claim: In the unstable condition, the rewarded target always appeared at the location of the best target, and the hazard rate was high (H = 0.35).
source: In the unstable condition (Figure 1D–E), the rewarded target always appeared at the location of the best target, and the hazard rate was high (H = 0.35).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the parameters of the unstable condition and references Figure 1D-E.

claim: Participants learned the location of the best target after a change in its location more quickly and reliably in the unstable than the noisy condition.
source: On average, they learned the location of the best target after a change in its location more quickly and reliably in the unstable than the noisy condition (Figure 2A).
evidence: The manuscript reports behavioral results comparing learning rates between conditions, with reference to Figure 2A.

claim: Target switches tended to follow errors of any magnitude in the unstable condition but only errors of high magnitude in the noisy condition.
source: First, target switches (i.e. predicting a different target than on the previous trial) tended to follow errors of any magnitude in the unstable condition but only errors of high magnitude (i.e. when the chosen target was 3, 4, or five targets away from the rewarded target) in the noisy condition (sign test for H0: equal probability of switching for the two conditions; error magnitude of 1: median = −0.35, interquartile range (IQR) = [−0.62,–0.25], p<0.001; error magnitude of 2: median = −0.30, IQR = [−0.70,–0.11], p<0.001; Figure 2B–C).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical tests comparing switch probabilities between conditions for different error magnitudes.

claim: Target switches depended on error history only for low-magnitude errors in the noisy condition but not otherwise.
source: Second, target switches depended on error history only for low-magnitude errors (i.e. when the chosen target was 1 or two targets away from the rewarded target) in the noisy condition but not otherwise (sign test for H0: switching was unaffected when recent history contained fewer errors; error magnitude of 1: median = −0.29, IQR = [−0.42,–0.10], p=0.004; error magnitude of 2: median = −0.25, IQR = [−0.38,–0.14], p<0.001; Figure 2D–F).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical tests showing the effect of error history on switching behavior.

claim: A reduced Bayesian model accounted for participants' behavioral patterns.
source: We accounted for these behavioral patterns with a reduced Bayesian model that is similar to ones we have used previously to model belief updating in a dynamic environment (open symbols in Figure 2; Tables 1 and 2).
evidence: The manuscript states that the reduced Bayesian model was used to account for behavior, with references to figures and tables.

claim: The fitted hazard rates were higher in the unstable condition than in the noisy condition.
source: As expected, the fitted hazard rates were higher in the unstable condition than in the noisy condition, although both tended to be higher than the objective values, as we have observed previously (Nassar et al., 2010).
evidence: The manuscript reports model fitting results comparing hazard rates between conditions and cites previous work.

claim: The fitted noise estimates were not reliably different between the noisy and unstable conditions.
source: However, the fitted noise estimates were not reliably different between the noisy and unstable conditions (Table 2).
evidence: The manuscript reports model fitting results for noise estimates with reference to Table 2.

claim: The subjective estimates of noise level were high in the unstable condition despite the objective absence of noise.
source: As we observed in our previous study (Li et al., 2019), the subjective estimates of noise level were high in the unstable condition despite the objective absence of noise.
evidence: The manuscript reports model fitting results and cites previous work.

claim: Activity positively correlated with the levels of CPP and RU was found across DLPFC and PPC.
source: Similar to our previous study, we found activity that was positively correlated with the levels of CPP and RU across DLPFC and PPC (Figure 2—figure supplements 3 and 4).
evidence: The manuscript reports fMRI results with reference to supplementary figures.

claim: Task-dependent representations of error magnitude were found in posterior parietal cortex.
source: Using multi-voxel pattern classification, we identified task-dependent representations of error magnitude and past errors in posterior parietal cortex.
evidence: The manuscript reports MVPA results identifying brain regions encoding error information.

claim: Task-dependent representations of past errors were found in posterior parietal cortex.
source: Using multi-voxel pattern classification, we identified task-dependent representations of error magnitude and past errors in posterior parietal cortex.
evidence: The manuscript reports MVPA results identifying brain regions encoding error information.

claim: Representations of behavioral adjustments were found in dorsomedial frontal, anterior cingulate, and orbitofrontal cortex.
source: These representations were distinct from representations of the resulting behavioral adjustments in dorsomedial frontal, anterior cingulate, and orbitofrontal cortex.
evidence: The manuscript reports MVPA results identifying brain regions encoding behavioral adjustments.

claim: The representation of error magnitude was stronger in the noisy than the unstable condition in PPC.
source: Consistent with the task-dependent behavioral effects, this representation of error magnitude was stronger in the noisy than the unstable condition (Figure 3 and Table 3).
evidence: The manuscript reports MVPA results comparing error magnitude encoding between conditions.

claim: Error magnitude could be classified only for the noisy condition and most strongly in the lateral and medial parietal cortex and in the occipital pole.
source: However, for error trials, we could classify error magnitude (in three bins: 1, 2, 3+ targets away from the rewarded target) only for the noisy condition and most strongly in the lateral and medial parietal cortex and in the occipital pole.
evidence: The manuscript reports MVPA classification results for error magnitude.

claim: Univariate activity in PPC varied in a task-dependent way, responding more strongly to error magnitude in the noisy than the unstable condition.
source: In a parallel set of analyses, we found that univariate activity in PPC also varied in a task-dependent way, responding more strongly to error magnitude in the noisy than the unstable condition (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports univariate fMRI analysis results with reference to a supplementary figure.

claim: Representations of past errors in PPC were stronger in the noisy than the unstable condition, particularly on trials for which past errors had the strongest influence on behavior.
source: These representations also were stronger in the noisy than the unstable condition, particularly on trials for which past errors had the strongest influence on behavior.
evidence: The manuscript reports MVPA results comparing past error encoding between conditions.

claim: Past errors could be classified in the lateral and medial parietal cortex in both conditions for correct trials and trials with error magnitudes of 0 or 3+.
source: We found reliable classifications of past errors in the lateral and medial parietal cortex in both conditions for correct trials and trials with error magnitudes of 0 or 3+.
evidence: The manuscript reports MVPA classification results for past errors.

claim: Representations of past errors were stronger for error trials and trials with error magnitudes of 1 or two in the noisy than in the unstable condition.
source: Moreover, these representations depended on the current condition, and, consistent with behavioral effects of error history, were stronger for error trials and trials with error magnitudes of 1 or two in the noisy than in the unstable condition (Table 3).
evidence: The manuscript reports MVPA results comparing past error encoding between conditions with reference to Table 3.

claim: PPC uniquely encoded task-dependent error signals for both error magnitude of the current trials and past errors when the current trial's error magnitude was 1 or 2.
source: An additional conjunction analysis across MVPA results showed that PPC uniquely encoded task-dependent error signals for both error magnitude of the current trials and past errors when the current trial's error magnitude was 1 or 2 (Table 3).
evidence: The manuscript reports conjunction analysis results with reference to Table 3.

claim: Activity patterns in motor cortex, OFC, ACC, DMFC, and DLPFC could predict subsequent stay/switch decisions.
source: We found that activity patterns in large cluster encompassing motor cortex, OFC, ACC, DMFC, and DLPFC could predict subsequent stay/switch decisions (Figure 5, Table 4).
evidence: The manuscript reports MVPA results predicting behavioral choices with references to Figure 5 and Table 4.

claim: No regions showed univariate activity that reliably predicted participants' subsequent behavior.
source: We did not find any regions where univariate activity reliably predicted participants' subsequent behavior (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The manuscript reports null results from univariate analysis with reference to a supplementary figure.

claim: Errors often drive adaptive adjustments in beliefs that inform behaviors that maximize positive outcomes and minimize negative ones.
source: Errors often drive adaptive adjustments in beliefs that inform behaviors that maximize positive outcomes and minimize negative ones (Sutton and Barto, 1998).
evidence: The manuscript states this as background knowledge and cites a reference.

claim: Errors can arise from different sources that have different implications for learning in uncertain and dynamic environments.
source: A major challenge to error-driven learning in uncertain and dynamic environments is that errors can arise from different sources that have different implications for learning.
evidence: The manuscript presents this as a conceptual framework for the study.

claim: Errors that represent fundamental changes in the environment or that occur during periods of uncertainty should probably lead to belief updates and behavior changes.
source: In general, errors that represent fundamental changes in the environment or that occur during periods of uncertainty should probably lead you to update your beliefs and change your behavior, whereas those that result from environmental stochasticity are likely better ignored (d'Acremont and Bossaerts, 2016; Li et al., 2019; Nassar et al., 2019a; O'Reilly et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript presents this principle with citations to support it.

claim: Errors that result from environmental stochasticity are likely better ignored.
source: In general, errors that represent fundamental changes in the environment or that occur during periods of uncertainty should probably lead you to update your beliefs and change your behavior, whereas those that result from environmental stochasticity are likely better ignored (d'Acremont and Bossaerts, 2016; Li et al., 2019; Nassar et al., 2019a; O'Reilly et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript presents this principle with citations to support it.

claim: Correlates of change-point probability and relative uncertainty have been identified in dorsomedial frontal and dorsolateral prefrontal cortex and medial and lateral posterior parietal cortex.
source: Correlates of these variables have been identified in dorsomedial frontal (DMFC) and dorsolateral prefrontal (DLPFC) cortex and medial and lateral posterior parietal cortex (PPC) (Behrens et al., 2007; McGuire et al., 2014; Nassar et al., 2019a).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies that identified these neural correlates.

claim: PPC has a role in error monitoring based on representations of surprise induced by state changes or outliers.
source: These and other studies also suggest specific roles for these different brain regions in error-driving learning, including representations of surprise induced by either state changes or outliers (irrelevant to state changes) in the PPC that suggest a role in error monitoring (Nassar et al., 2019a; O'Reilly et al., 2013), and representations of variables more closely related to belief and behavior updating in the prefrontal cortex (PFC) (McGuire et al., 2014; O'Reilly et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies suggesting this role for PPC.

claim: Prefrontal cortex has representations of variables more closely related to belief and behavior updating.
source: These and other studies also suggest specific roles for these different brain regions in error-driving learning, including representations of surprise induced by either state changes or outliers (irrelevant to state changes) in the PPC that suggest a role in error monitoring (Nassar et al., 2019a; O'Reilly et al., 2013), and representations of variables more closely related to belief and behavior updating in the prefrontal cortex (PFC) (McGuire et al., 2014; O'Reilly et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies suggesting this role for PFC.

claim: Previous studies were not designed to identify neural signals related to responding to the same kinds of errors differently in different conditions.
source: However, these previous studies, which typically used continuous rather than discrete feedback, were not designed to identify neural signals related to a key aspect of flexible learning in uncertain and dynamic environments: responding to the same kinds of errors differently in different conditions.
evidence: The manuscript identifies a gap in previous research.

claim: The paradigm was adapted from a previous single-unit recording study.
source: To identify such task-dependent neural responses to errors, we adapted a paradigm from our previous single-unit recording study (Li et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript cites the source of the paradigm.

claim: In the previous single-unit recording study, many single neurons in ACC or PCC responded to errors or the current condition.
source: In our previous study, we found many single neurons in the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) or posterior cingulate cortex (PCC) that responded to errors or the current condition, but we found little evidence that single neurons in these regions combined this information in a task-dependent manner to discriminate the source of errors or drive behavior.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes findings from a previous study.

claim: Little evidence was found that single neurons in ACC or PCC combined error and condition information in a task-dependent manner.
source: In our previous study, we found many single neurons in the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) or posterior cingulate cortex (PCC) that responded to errors or the current condition, but we found little evidence that single neurons in these regions combined this information in a task-dependent manner to discriminate the source of errors or drive behavior.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes findings from a previous study.

claim: The results provide new insights into how the human brain represents errors in a task-dependent manner and guides subsequent adaptive behavior.
source: The results provide new insights into how the human brain represents errors in a task-dependent manner and guides subsequent adaptive behavior.
evidence: The manuscript states this as a conclusion in the abstract.

claim: Human participants adapted their response to errors differently in different environments.
source: Consistent with previous studies of ours and others (d'Acremont and Bossaerts, 2016; McGuire et al., 2014; Nassar et al., 2019a; Nassar et al., 2012; Nassar et al., 2010; O'Reilly et al., 2013; Purcell and Kiani, 2016), human participants adapted their response to errors differently in different environments.
evidence: The manuscript reports behavioral findings consistent with previous work.

claim: In the unstable condition, participants almost always switched their choice after errors and quickly learned the new state after change-points.
source: In the unstable condition, participants almost always switched their choice after errors and quickly learned the new state after change-points.
evidence: The manuscript reports behavioral results for the unstable condition.

claim: In the noisy condition, participants ignored many errors and only slowly learned the new state after change-points.
source: In contrast, in the noisy condition, participants ignored many errors and only slowly learned the new state after change-points.
evidence: The manuscript reports behavioral results for the noisy condition.

claim: In the noisy condition, participants used error magnitude and recent error history as a cue for whether the state had recently changed or not.
source: In this condition, participants had to distinguish true change-points from environmental noise, and they used error magnitude and recent error history as a cue for whether the state had recently changed or not.
evidence: The manuscript reports behavioral results for the noisy condition.

claim: The reduced Bayesian model assumes that participants use approximately optimal inference processes but can have subjective estimates of environmental parameters that depart from their true values.
source: This model assumes that participants use approximately optimal inference processes but can have subjective estimates of environmental parameters (hazard rate, noise) that depart from their true values.
evidence: The manuscript describes the assumptions of the reduced Bayesian model.

claim: CPP accounts for task-dependent behavioral responses to error magnitude in the reduced Bayesian model.
source: Thus, CPP and RU each account for one of the two key signatures of task-dependent learning that we identified in participants' behavior, with CPP driving a task-dependent influence of error magnitude and RU driving a task-dependent influence of error history on target switches.
evidence: The manuscript explains the role of CPP in the model.

claim: RU accounts for task-dependent behavioral responses to error history in the reduced Bayesian model.
source: Thus, CPP and RU each account for one of the two key signatures of task-dependent learning that we identified in participants' behavior, with CPP driving a task-dependent influence of error magnitude and RU driving a task-dependent influence of error history on target switches.
evidence: The manuscript explains the role of RU in the model.

claim: The replication of CPP and RU neural representations shows the robustness of these representations across experimental designs that differ dramatically in their visual stimuli and motor demands.
source: This replication shows the robustness of these neural representations of CPP and RU across experimental designs that differ dramatically in their visual stimuli and motor demands, yet share the need to learn in dynamic environments with similar statistics.
evidence: The manuscript interprets the replication of previous findings.

claim: PPC has been shown previously to represent errors, error magnitudes, surprise and salience.
source: These same regions of PPC have been shown previously to represent errors, error magnitudes, surprise and salience (Fischer and Ullsperger, 2013; Gläscher et al., 2010; McGuire et al., 2014; Nassar et al., 2019a; Nassar et al., 2019b; O'Reilly et al., 2013; Payzan-LeNestour et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies showing these representations in PPC.

claim: PPC has been shown to integrate recent outcome or stimulus history in human fMRI studies and in animal single neuron recording studies.
source: In addition, these regions have been shown to integrate recent outcome or stimulus history in human fMRI studies (FitzGerald et al., 2015; Furl and Averbeck, 2011) and in animal single neuron recording studies (Akrami et al., 2018; Brody and Hanks, 2016; Hanks et al., 2015; Hayden et al., 2008; Hwang et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies showing history integration in PPC.

claim: The whole-brain fMRI results complement previous results recording from single neurons in ACC and PCC in the same task.
source: These whole-brain fMRI results complement our previous results recording from single neurons in ACC and PCC in the same task (Li et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript relates current findings to previous work.

claim: PPC would be a good place to look for task-dependent error representations in single neurons.
source: Our whole-brain fMRI results suggest that PPC would be a good place to look for task-dependent error representations in single neurons, including a region of medial parietal cortex slightly dorsal to the PCC area we recorded from previously.
evidence: The manuscript makes a prediction based on current findings.

claim: The multivariate pattern in frontal cortex, particularly ACC and medial PFC, can decode subsequent switching versus staying in a reversal learning task.
source: These results extend previous findings that the multivariate pattern in frontal cortex, particularly ACC and medial PFC, can decode subsequent switching versus staying in a reversal learning task (Hampton and O'doherty, 2007).
evidence: The manuscript cites a previous study showing this decoding ability.

claim: The results suggest a dissociation between PPC regions that monitor error information in a task-dependent manner and frontal regions that may use this information to update beliefs and select subsequent actions.
source: These results suggest a dissociation between PPC regions that monitor error information in a task-dependent manner and frontal regions that may use this information to update beliefs and select subsequent actions.
evidence: The manuscript interprets the findings to suggest functional dissociation.

claim: Medial PFC is involved in performance monitoring, distinguishing errors from different sources such as actions and feedback.
source: Medial PFC is involved in performance monitoring, distinguishing errors from different sources such as actions and feedback (Ullsperger et al., 2014), registering a hierarchy of prediction errors from those due to environmental noise to those due to a change in the environmental state (Alexander and Brown, 2015), and interacting with lateral PFC to guide subsequent behavioral adjustments in response to errors (Alexander and Brown, 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies describing the role of medial PFC.

claim: Activity in DMFC reflects the extent of belief updating in dynamic environments.
source: Consistent with this role, activity in DMFC also reflects the extent of belief updating in dynamic environments (Behrens et al., 2007; Hampton et al., 2006; McGuire et al., 2014; O'Reilly et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies describing the role of DMFC.

claim: OFC and DMFC encode the identity of the current latent state in a mental model of the task environment.
source: OFC and DMFC encode the identity of the current latent state in a mental model of the task environment and neural representations in these regions changes as the state changes (Chan et al., 2016; Hunt et al., 2018; Karlsson et al., 2012; Nassar et al., 2019b; Schuck et al., 2016; Wilson et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies describing the role of OFC and DMFC.

claim: Activity in inferior frontal junction reflects the updating of task representations.
source: Activity in inferior frontal junction reflects the updating of task representations (Brass and von Cramon, 2004; Derrfuss et al., 2005).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies describing the role of inferior frontal junction.

claim: Neural activity in frontopolar cortex and DMFC increases during exploratory choices.
source: Neural activity in frontopolar cortex (Daw et al., 2006) and DMFC (Blanchard and Gershman, 2018; Kolling et al., 2012; Kolling et al., 2016; Muller et al., 2019) increases during exploratory choices, which occur more frequently during periods of uncertainty about the most beneficial option.
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies describing neural activity during exploration.

claim: Distinct representations of latent states, uncertainty, and behavioral policy were identified in distinct areas of frontal cortex during learning in a dynamic environment.
source: In a recent study, we identified distinct representations of latent states, uncertainty, and behavioral policy in distinct areas of frontal cortex during learning in a dynamic environment (Nassar et al., 2019b).
evidence: The manuscript cites a previous study identifying these representations.

claim: The study had a relatively small number of participants (n = 16).
source: First, we had relatively small number of participants in this study (n = 16).
evidence: The manuscript acknowledges this limitation.

claim: False-positive rates were controlled through permutation tests that have been validated empirically.
source: Although we control the false-positive rates through permutation tests that have been validated empirically (Eklund et al., 2016), it is possible that we lacked the statistical power to detect some effects, and so null results should be interpreted with caution.
evidence: The manuscript describes the statistical approach and cites validation.

claim: Two qualitatively different task conditions were created by manipulating both the noise levels and hazard rates.
source: Second, in this study, we created two qualitatively different task conditions by manipulating both the noise levels and hazard rates.
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental design.

claim: Behavioral or neural differences across conditions cannot be attributed specifically to changes in either noise levels or hazard rates alone.
source: Thus, we cannot attribute any behavioral or neural differences across conditions specifically to changes in either noise levels or hazard rates alone, but rather to how the combinations of these two variables affect the interpretation and use of small errors.
evidence: The manuscript acknowledges this limitation of the experimental design.

claim: In PPC, neural patterns encoded error information in a task-dependent manner, depending on error magnitude and past errors only under conditions where these were informative of the source of error.
source: In PPC, neural patterns encoded error information in a task-dependent manner, depending on error magnitude and past errors only under conditions where these were informative of the source of error.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes the main findings.

claim: Activity in frontal cortex could predict subsequent choices that could be based on error information.
source: In contrast, activity in frontal cortex could predict subsequent choices that could be based on this information.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes the main findings.

claim: The findings suggest a broad distinction between outcome monitoring in parietal regions and action selection in frontal regions when learning in dynamic and uncertain environments.
source: These findings suggest a broad distinction between outcome monitoring in parietal regions and action selection in frontal regions when learning in dynamic and uncertain environments.
evidence: The manuscript states this as a conclusion.

source: All procedures were approved by University of Pennsylvania Internal Review Board.
evidence: The manuscript states ethical approval.

source: One additional participant was excluded from analyses because of large head movements during MRI scanning (>10% of timepoint-to-timepoint displacements were >0.5 mm).
evidence: The manuscript reports participant exclusion criteria.

claim: All participants provided informed consent before the experiment.
source: All participants provided informed consent before the experiment.
evidence: The manuscript states ethical procedures.

source: Participants received a participation fee of $15, as well as extra incentives based on their performance (mean = $15.09, SD = $2.26, range = $8.5–17.5).
evidence: The manuscript reports participant compensation.

claim: There were 300 trials in each run.
source: There were 300 trials in each run.
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental design.

source: First, we removed trials in which participants did not make a choice within the time limit (Unstable: median number of trials = 10.5, range = 1–83; Noisy: median = 10, range = 2–88).

source: Second, we also removed trials in which the location of the chosen target was not on the shortest distance between the previously chosen and previously rewarded targets (Unstable: median = 3, range = 0–24; Noisy: median = 17, range = 5–37).

claim: All of the belief-updating models tested predict that participants' choice should be along the shortest distance between the previously chosen target and the previously rewarded target.
source: All of the belief-updating models we tested predict that participants' choice should be along the shortest distance between the previously chosen target and the previously rewarded target.

source: The analysis codes were written in MATLAB and are available at Github (Kao, 2020; https://github.com/changhaokao/mvpa_changepoint_fmri).
evidence: The manuscript provides information about code availability.

source: Previous studies have shown that a reduced Bayesian model, which approximates the full Bayesian ideal observer, could account well for participants' behavior in dynamic environments similar to the current task (McGuire et al., 2014; Nassar et al., 2012; Nassar et al., 2010).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies describing the model.

source: Each model was fitted to data from each participant and within each condition separately.

source: We acquired MRI data on a 3T Siemens Prisma with a 64-channel head coil.
